tagline.text: A waterfall in a limestone gorge in Samboan's Barangay Suba, reached by walking and wading up a river

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–700 (entrance, guide, and parking; transport extra)

children.text: Dao Falls is a waterfall in Barangay Suba, Samboan, in southwestern Cebu, reached by walking up a gorge between limestone walls and crossing the river several times. A guide is required, and the fee information differs by source, so check locally.

Dao Falls (some sources spell it Dau Falls) is in Suba, a hill barangay of Samboan, a coastal town on the southwest of Cebu Island. From the coastal road you climb a narrow, palm-lined road to the parking area, and from there you walk down into the gorge. Reported heights vary widely, from a tall waterfall of several dozen meters to about 120 m, so think of it simply as a big waterfall dropping between limestone cliffs rather than relying on a number. It is often counted among the most beautiful falls in Samboan. The water comes from the outflow of Candayvic Falls upstream and drops over a nearly vertical limestone wall into a round, turquoise basin. One guide says the shape resembles a giant ladle, which gave the falls their name.

The way there is not difficult, but expect to get wet. From the starting point you descend roughly 200 steps to the gorge floor and cross a bamboo bridge along the way. After that you walk along the river and cross it several times, usually in ankle-deep water. It takes about 30–40 minutes one way, longer if you stop for photos. Near the falls you climb stairs built by local people, and the limestone walls around the falls cannot be climbed. The path is slippery after rain, so think carefully about your footwear. The gorge path passes a wooden bridge near the start and follows the river between two limestone walls; the small cascade above the main falls is off limits, and swimming is said to be allowed only in the basin below the falls and in rock pools along the trail.

Entrance fees differ by source. Older posts mention around ₱20, others ₱100, and up to ₱200 including a guide, helmet, and neoprene shoes, while parking is listed at ₱20 for a motorbike and ₱50 for a car. Sources disagree on whether a guide is required or optional, but recent ones lean toward required. Some reviewers say guides ask for tips, so carry small bills in cash. A tip of about ₱50 for the guide is said to be common. Figures from 2025 and February 2026 give ₱200 per person with a guide included.

Opening hours are reported as roughly 06:00–15:00 (one guide says 07:00–16:30), and the gorge darkens early in the afternoon, so go in the morning. One review says there were few people around lunchtime, while another notes that peak-season weekends get crowded. There is no restaurant at the falls or the parking area, only snacks and drinks, and a few restaurants sit along the main road. Overnight stays and camping are reportedly not allowed. Two travel blogs (a February 2025 report and a guide updated April 2026) say the falls are reportedly closed on Mondays for weekly clearing, but no official notice has been confirmed, so avoiding Mondays is the safe choice. A sign at Dao Eskina is said to show about 1.2 km to the falls. Tumalog Falls in nearby Oslob is reported to close from 28 October 2026, so check that when planning southern Cebu. Samboan lies about 150 km south of Cebu City on the Tañon Strait, and because it is hard to fit into an Oslob or Kawasan Falls itinerary it stays quiet and uncrowded. Many visitors therefore pair the falls with the coral-stone church in the town center, the Spanish watchtower, and the 147 steps of Jacob's Ladder for a full day.

blocks.title: A Waterfall in a Limestone Gorge

children.text: The falls are enclosed by limestone walls that cannot be climbed, and the gorge leads through forest, turquoise water, and rock pools. Some stretches have only small drops and are good for splashing about.

blocks.title: A Trek That Crosses the River

children.text: The gorge path crosses the river many times, so be ready to get wet. The water is usually ankle deep but rises in the rainy season.
You descend about 200 steps at the start and cross a bamboo bridge partway. At the end you climb stairs built by residents to reach the base of the falls.

blocks.title: A Shallow Pool at the Falls

children.text: The pool below the falls is generally shallow and is described as popular with families with children. The water is fullest around the rainy season.

Samboan has many waterfalls. Aguinid Falls, Hidden Binalayan Falls, Candayvic Falls, Calasa Falls, and San Miguel Falls are among those mentioned, and there is also a route of about 40 minutes on foot from Candayvic Falls to Dao Falls. Whether a guide is needed differs from place to place, so confirm locally.
Samboan has a white-sand beach, Lambug, that is good for a rest after the falls. Snorkeling is best at high tide, and it is said to be visited mostly by locals.

In Samboan town there is a coral-stone church and a three-story Spanish watchtower. They are good to see in the afternoon after the falls, and the 147 steps from the church toward the coast are said to have fine sea views.
Set out from your accommodation in Moalboal or Samboan and ride along the coastal road, turning up at the Dao sign.
Park, pay the entrance fee, and walk down the stairs with your guide.

Reach the falls for photos and a splash.
There are many steps on the way back, so climb slowly.
Have lunch at a restaurant on the main road.
The gorge loses sunlight early, so we recommend a morning visit.
Leave Moalboal by motorbike or car. It is about 53 km, around 1 hour 30 minutes by motorbike.
Park at Dao Falls and go down into the gorge with your guide.
Climb back up and have lunch on the main road.
Stop at other waterfalls or a beach in Samboan and head back before dark.
Reviews say the falls close on Mondays, so we recommend going Tuesday through Sunday.

If you drive, parking is close to the starting point and the road is mostly concrete with some dirt sections. The road is narrow, with stretches where two motorbikes barely pass, so watch for oncoming traffic.
The dry season from December to April is relatively stable and the water is clear. From May to November the rains thicken the flow, but the gorge path is slippery and the river rises.
Mornings are best. The gorge darkens early in the afternoon and more people arrive.

The water is fullest in the rainy season, but after heavy rain the river in the gorge can rise and make the path dangerous, so talk with your guide and change your plans if the weather is bad. In the dry season the flow drops but the pools remain good for swimming. Holidays and peak-season weekends are busier, so weekday mornings are recommended.

Moalboal offers the widest choice of places to stay. Samboan itself has a few small lodgings but fewer options, so check ahead.
There is no restaurant near the falls. Restaurants such as Happy Bowl + Cafe, Lucky 9ers, and Tuslob Buwa are mentioned along the main road, but confirm they are open locally.

Samboan is a town along the southern Cebu coastal road, and many visitors reach the falls by motorbike from Moalboal. Reviews mention rentals at about ₱350–400 a day, but rates differ by shop, so confirm.

The hill with the Church of St. Michael the Archangel is the center of Samboan town, so after the falls it is pleasant to stroll to the church and watchtower. To see both the falls and the church hill in one day, visit the falls first thing in the morning and walk through town in the afternoon. A day trip from Cebu City involves a long ride, so we recommend using a whole day or staying a night in Moalboal or Samboan.
Wear clothes that can get wet and shoes with good grip.

Going early is quieter and the gorge is brighter.

The small cascade above the main falls is off limits.
Rather than rushing back after the falls, plan a relaxed afternoon in town.
If a day trip feels too long, we recommend one night in Moalboal or Samboan.
The gorge path is very slippery after rain and the river can rise, so change your plans in bad weather and confirm guide rules and fees locally.
